analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $7.25 and restores overtime pay for workers newly excluded by a 2004 rule.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat on the Senate calendar for the rest of the 109th Congress and died when that Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the federal minimum wage in three steps to $7.25 an hour. It would also cancel the parts of a 2004 Labor Department rule that removed overtime pay from workers who had qualified under the older rules, and raise and index the salary threshold for overtime exemptions. It includes a non-binding statement supporting multiemployer pension plans. It was placed on the Senate calendar but never debated or voted on.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers earning near the minimum wage would get phased raises to $7.25 an hour. Workers who lost overtime eligibility under the April 2004 rule would get it back, and the salary cutoff for overtime exemptions would rise from its 1975 level of $155 a week to $591 a week and keep pace with wage growth afterward.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $5.85, then $6.55, then $7.25 an hour in steps over roughly two years.

Strikes down the portions of the April 23, 2004 overtime rule that made employees exempt who would not have been exempt under the regulations in effect on March 31, 2003, restoring their right to overtime pay.

Raises the minimum salary level for white-collar overtime exemptions from $155 per week (set in 1975) to $591 per week, with automatic annual increases tied to the Employment Cost Index so the threshold does not erode again.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay minimum wage or rely on the 2004 overtime exemptions would pay higher wages and overtime. Low-wage industries such as retail and restaurants would bear the largest payroll increases.

drawbacks.text: The wage increase is a mandate on employers, and small businesses with thin margins could respond by cutting hours, slowing hiring, or raising prices.
Reinstating the pre-2003 overtime rules by statute, rather than through the usual rulemaking process, removes the Labor Department's flexibility to update exemptions to fit changing workplaces.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are direct and large for the workers affected: higher base pay and restored overtime. The costs fall on the employers who pay those wages, mostly in low-wage sectors, and some of that cost can show up as reduced hours or higher prices. On balance the bill is a straightforward wage transfer from employers to low-paid workers, with a modest design question about fixing overtime rules in statute.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and placed on the Senate's calendar of pending business, but no one ever brought it up for debate or a vote, and it died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on April 19, 2005, and it was read the first time and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar the same day.
On April 20, 2005, it was read a second time and placed on the Senate calendar under General Orders, Calendar No. 80, which is where bills wait until the majority leader brings them to the floor.
The bill received one cosponsor and no committee action, and the Senate never debated or voted on it; it expired with the 109th Congress on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have owed higher minimum wages and restored overtime came out ahead, because the 2004 overtime exemptions stayed in force and the minimum wage remained $5.15. Low-wage workers gained nothing from this bill.

for.name: Richard J. Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise the minimum wage and restore overtime protections, and put it on the Senate calendar.

for.name: One Senate Democrat
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; it drew no other cosponsors in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Senate Majority Leader and floor leadership, 109th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never called the bill up from the Senate calendar for debate or a vote during the remainder of the 109th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only sponsors were Democrats (Durbin plus one cosponsor), and with Republicans controlling the Senate the bill never reached the floor, so no vote ever showed where the chamber stood.

industries.note: Restaurants are the largest employer of minimum-wage workers and would have borne steep payroll increases as the wage rose to $7.25. The bill's failure kept their labor costs unchanged at workers' expense.
Large and small retailers paying near the minimum wage would have faced higher wage floors; the bill's death preserved the status quo for them.
Businesses that reclassified newly exempt workers under the April 2004 Labor Department rule would have had to restore overtime pay; blocking the bill kept those exemptions in place.
The bill's third title is only a non-binding Senate statement of support for multiemployer pension plans serving about 9.7 million workers and retirees; it changes no law for them.
